Understanding Physical Activity, Inactivity, and Sedentary

Behavior Terminology

+ Physically active: getting at least 150 minutes/week of moderate to vigorous
physical activity (MVPA)

+ Insufficiently physically active: getting > 0 and < 150 minutes/week of MVPA

+ Physically inactive: getting 0 minutes/week of MVPA

- Important note: Many research studies and the Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention and World Health Organization guidelines classify physical
activity as a binary variable. This means that people are classified as either
physically active if they meet the 150 minutes/week of MVPA or physically
inactive if they get < 150 minutes/week of MVPA.

- While this is helpful from a research standpoint, from a clinical standpoint,
there is tremendous value in performing even small amounts of MVPA and not
viewing 150 minutes/week as a mandatory threshold.

» Benefits of MVPA accrue immediately with any level of activity and are
relatively greater the less active someone is at baseline.
+ Sedentary behavior: any waking behavior characterized by a low energy
expenditure < 1.5 metabolic equivalents of tasks, while in a seated, reclined, or
lying posture

Fitness: The ability to perform the activities of daily life, respond to emergencies, and enjoy leisure
time activities with sufficient energy and vitality and without excess fatigue. It is the outcome of

cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, and flexibility. It is
associated with lower prevalence of chronic disease, health conditions, and their risk factors.

2. Skill-related fitness: The components of physical activity related to movements necessary to
demonstrate a variety of motor skills and movement patterns, including agility, coordination,
balance, power, reaction time, and speed.

Deconditioning*”°

1. Astate of health that occurs from consistent physical inactivity and lack of exercise in daily life,
which results in functional loss.

2. Deconditioning is a common, preventable cause of morbidity and mortality.’7*

Progressive overload: Gradually increasing weight, frequency, or number of repetitions in a strength

routine to challenge the musculoskeletal system to adapt to challenging stimuli.

Specificity: The way the body responds to physical activity is specific to the activity itself—for

example, someone who jogs should expect that their jogging performance and aerobic conditioning

would improve with time. However, this does not mean that performance in other aerobic activities,
such as cycling, will improve, nor should they expect muscular strength or flexibility to improve.

Reversibility: When a person stops exercising, they lose the effects of training.

Principle of individuality: No two individuals will benefit from exercise exactly the same way, either

physically or psychologically.

GLOSSARY

Aerobic/endurance exercise (cardiovascular): the body's large muscles moving in rhythmic manner for a
sustained period of time.

Balance: the ability to withstand destabilizing stimuli (especially important with age).
Body composition: the percentages of body water, bone, muscle, and fat.

Borg scale: a rating of perceived exertion (RPE) used to monitor intensity of exercise. The short version
ranges from 1 to 10.

Cardiorespiratory endurance: the ability to continue aerobic exercise like walking or running.

Deconditioning: a state of health that occurs from being consistently physically inactive and lacking
exercise in one’s daily life, all of which results in functional losses.

Dynamic stretching: stretching with slow movement through a progressive range of motion and repeated
movements.

Exercise: purposeful physical activity that is organized, planned, reoccurring, and that is done with the intent
of improving or maintaining one or more components of one's health.

Exercise tolerance test (ETT): an exercise stress test that tests for cardiovascular fitness.

FIT T-VP: a type of exercise prescription that includes recommendations on frequency, intensity, type of
exercise, time, volume, and progression.

Flexibility: the ability to move a joint closer to its full range of motion.

Health-Related Fitness: a component of physical fitness that emphasizes the ability to perform activities of
daily living with vigor. There is a focus on the assessment of body composition, cardiorespiratory endurance,
muscular strength, muscular endurance, and flexibility. Health-related fitness is associated with lower
prevalence of chronic disease and associated risk factors.
